# The Paradox of the Politically-Sophisticated Partisan: The French Case

Sally Marthaler Correspondence S.A.Marthaler@sussex.ac.uk 

 Pages 937-959 | Published online: 26 Aug 2008

- Cite this article 
- https://doi.org/10.1080/01402380802234607

## Abstract

The erosion of partisan ties observed in many advanced industrialised democracies has been attributed to a cluster of factors associated with societal modernisation. This article considers the impact of one of these explanatory factors, the political sophistication of the electorate, in the case of France. Specifically, it tests the proposition that a more highly-educated and better-informed electorate will be less partisan. Its findings challenge a number of the assumptions behind the ‘independent’ voter thesis. The evidence points to the fact that it is lower rather than higher cognitive mobilisation that is associated with apartisanship. More politically-sophisticated voters, young and old alike, tend to have stronger party attachment and to rely on this rather than on complex evaluations of issues and policy to guide their voting decision.

## Notes

1. The 1978 and 1997 surveys relate to parliamentary elections, the 1988 survey to the presidential election and all three are post-election surveys. In 2002, a panel study was conducted in three waves covering both the presidential and parliamentary elections. In this article, the 2002 data are drawn from the first wave pre-election survey since the post-election data are likely to have been contaminated by the singular circumstances of these elections, when the unexpected success of Le Pen in the first round of the presidential election produced an exceptional reaction among the electorate.

2. Semi-structured face-to-face interviews were carried out between April and July 2002 with 33 voters in Paris from a sample drawn from the electoral register of the 14th arrondissement. A further ten interviews were conducted in July 2002 with a random sample of voters in Saint-Denis in the banlieues north of Paris. The interviewees, while not representative of the French electorate as a whole, included a cross-section of the population in terms of gender, age, ethnicity, political affiliation, education and occupation.

3. For further analysis of cognition and affect as the bases of partisan feelings, see Weisberg and Greene (Citation 2003).

4. Strength of party attachment is measured by responses to a CEVIPOF question on party proximity in which respondents are asked to say how close they feel to a political party on a four-point scale. The term party attachment is used rather than party identification in the French case since there are no questions in the CEVIPOF surveys equivalent to those used in, for example, American and British surveys to measure party identification (i.e. ‘Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as [a Republican/Conservative/etc.]?’).

5. Based on data from the European Values Surveys, 1981–84 and 1995–97, provided by the UK Data Archive at the University of Essex, and the European Values Study Integrated Dataset, 1999–2000, made available by the Zentralarchiv at the University of Cologne, Germany.

6. To construct the cognitive mobilisation index, each variable was coded into four categories (Level of education: 1 = university; 2 = baccalauréat; 3 = some secondary; 4 = primary or less; Interest in politics: 1 = very interested; 2 = fairly interested; 3 = not very interested; 4 = not at all interested) with a combined total of 2–5 indicating high cognitive mobilisation and 6–8 low cognitive mobilisation. 

It should be noted that, after a certain age, level of education no longer varies, whereas interest in politics may. Nonetheless, the cognitive mobilisation index gives important insights into longitudinal trends. In addition, a major focus of this article is on the younger section of the electorate.

7. All correlations are Spearman's rho. Significance levels are indicated as follows: *** = significant at the .01 level; ** = significant at the .05 level; * = significant at the .10 level.
